claim: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common malignant soft tissue sarcoma.
source: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common malignant soft tissue sarcoma (Hawkins et al., 2013; Keller and Guttridge, 2013; Hettmer et al., 2014) that arises due to a block in myogenic differentiation.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: RMS arises due to a block in myogenic differentiation.
source: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common malignant soft tissue sarcoma (Hawkins et al., 2013; Keller and Guttridge, 2013; Hettmer et al., 2014) that arises due to a block in myogenic differentiation.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Children with high risk RMS disease have poor prognosis with only 30% showing 5-year event-free survival.
source: Children with high risk disease have poor prognosis with only 30% showing 5-year event-free survival.
evidence: Statement of clinical outcome data from established knowledge

claim: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS) accounts for the majority (~60%) of all RMS cases.
source: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (ERMS) accounts for the majority (~60%) of all RMS cases.
evidence: Statement of epidemiological data from established knowledge

claim: No single genetic lesion is linked to ERMS.
source: No single genetic lesion is linked to ERMS but chromosome gains (chr 2, 8, 12, and 13) and loss of heterozygosity at 11p15.5 are characteristically seen (Shern et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Chromosome gains (chr 2, 8, 12, and 13) and loss of heterozygosity at 11p15.5 are characteristically seen in ERMS.
source: No single genetic lesion is linked to ERMS but chromosome gains (chr 2, 8, 12, and 13) and loss of heterozygosity at 11p15.5 are characteristically seen (Shern et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Recurrent mutations in ERMS include mutations in p53 (TP53), amplification of CDK4, upregulation of MYCN, and point mutations in RAS leading to its activation.
source: A few recurrent mutations occur in ERMS that include mutations in p53 (TP53), amplification of CDK4, upregulation of MYCN, and point mutations in RAS leading to its activation (Hawkins et al., 2013; Shern et al., 2014; Zhu and Davie, 2015; Skapek et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: EZH2 that mediates repressive histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) is upregulated and binds to muscle specific genes in ERMS.
source: Among these, EZH2 that mediates repressive histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) is upregulated and binds to muscle specific genes in ERMS.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about EZH2 function in ERMS

claim: Silencing of EZH2 increases both MyoD binding and transcription of target genes in ERMS.
source: Its silencing increases both MyoD binding and transcription of target genes (Ciarapica et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: HDAC inhibitors induce differentiation and reduce self-renewal and migratory capacity of ERMS by regulating Notch-1 and EphrinB1-mediated pathways.
source: Similarly, HDAC inhibitors have been found to induce differentiation and reduce self-renewal and migratory capacity of ERMS by regulating Notch-1 and EphrinB1-mediated pathways (Vleeshouwer-Neumann et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Overexpression of the lysine methyltransferase SUV39H1 suppresses tumor formation in KRASG12D-driven zebrafish model of ERMS.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of the lysine methyltransferase SUV39H1 suppresses tumor formation in KRASG12D-driven zebrafish model of ERMS (Albacker et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Double mutants lacking p53 and c-fos (Trp53-/-/Fos-/-) develop ERMS.
source: Double mutants lacking p53 and c-fos (Trp53-/-/Fos-/-) develop ERMS.
evidence: Statement of genetic model data from established knowledge

claim: Elevated expression of Wnt antagonists dickkopf-related protein 1 (DKK1) and secreted frizzled-related proteins (sFRPs), as well as downregulation of Wnt agonists such as Wnt ligands Wnt 7b, Wnt 5a, Wnt four, and Wnt 11 were reported in Trp53-/-/Fos-/- tumors.
source: Elevated expression of Wnt antagonists dickkopf-related protein 1 (DKK1) and secreted frizzled-related proteins (sFRPs), as well as downregulation of Wnt agonists such as Wnt ligands Wnt 7b, Wnt 5a, Wnt four, and Wnt 11 were reported in these tumors (Singh et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Mice expressing activated smoothened under the Fabp4 promoter leading to activation of Hedgehog signaling develop ERMS.
source: Mice expressing activated smoothened under the Fabp4 promoter leading to activation of Hedgehog signaling also develop ERMS.
evidence: Statement of genetic model data from established knowledge

claim: ERMS tumors from mice expressing activated smoothened show upregulation of Dkk3 which inhibits canonical Wnt signaling.
source: The tumors also show upregulation of Dkk3 which, similar to Dkk1, inhibits canonical Wnt signaling (Hatley et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: GSK3β inhibitors that activate Wnt signaling were most effective inducers of differentiation in a zebrafish model of ERMS.
source: Consistent with these findings, GSK3β inhibitors that activate Wnt signaling were most effective inducers of differentiation in a zebrafish model of ERMS (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Downregulation of Wnt signaling was found to be relevant only in ERMS.
source: Importantly downregulation of Wnt signaling was found to be relevant only in ERMS.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about Wnt signaling in RMS subtypes

claim: There are 19 Wnt ligands, which function either through the canonical or non-canonical pathways in a highly context-dependent manner.
source: There are 19 Wnt ligands, which function either through the canonical or non-canonical pathways in a highly context-dependent manner (Masuda and Ishitani, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling is activated when Wnt ligands bind to a receptor from the Frizzled (Fzd) family.
source: Canonical signaling is activated when Wnt ligands bind to a receptor from the Frizzled (Fzd) family.
evidence: Statement of established molecular mechanism

claim: The co-receptors LRP5/6 facilitate Wnt signaling.
source: The co-receptors LRP5/6 facilitate Wnt signaling.
evidence: Statement of established molecular mechanism

claim: Activation of Wnt signaling leads to disruption of the destruction complex (APC, Axin, GSK3β, and CK1α) which phosphorylates and degrades β-catenin.
source: Activation of Wnt signaling leads to disruption of the destruction complex (APC, Axin, GSK3β, and CK1α) which phosphorylates and degrades β-catenin.
evidence: Statement of established molecular mechanism

claim: Induction of Wnt signaling results in accumulation of non-phosphorylated β-catenin (active β-catenin).
source: Induction of Wnt signaling results in accumulation of non-phosphorylated β-catenin (active β-catenin).
evidence: Statement of established molecular mechanism

claim: β-catenin translocates to the nucleus where it activates genes in cooperation with TCF/LEF1, but also other transcription factors.
source: β-catenin then translocates to the nucleus where it activates genes in cooperation with TCF/LEF1, but also other transcription factors (Masuda and Ishitani, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Neither of the two non-canonical Wnt pathways (Planar Cell Polarity pathway [PCP] and the Wnt/calcium signaling pathway) involve β-catenin.
source: Neither of the two non-canonical pathways (Planar Cell Polarity pathway [PCP] and the Wnt/calcium signaling pathway) involve β-catenin.
evidence: Statement of established molecular mechanism

claim: Dkk1, a secreted protein, interacts with Lrp5/6 and antagonizes Wnt signaling by preventing Lrp5/6 association with Wnt/Fzd complex.
source: Dkk1, a secreted protein, interacts with Lrp5/6 and antagonizes Wnt signaling by preventing Lrp5/6 association with Wnt/Fzd complex (Niehrs, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: EHMT2, a lysine methyltransferase that is encoded by the EHTM2 gene, mediates mono and di-methylation of H3K9 (H3K9me1/2), which is primarily involved in transcriptional repression.
source: EHMT2, a lysine methyltransferase that is encoded by the EHTM2 gene, mediates mono and di-methylation of H3K9 (H3K9me1/2), which is primarily involved in transcriptional repression (Shinkai and Tachibana, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: EHMT2 can also function as an activator in methylation-independent and -dependent ways.
source: Recent studies however have shown that EHMT2 can also function as an activator in methylation-independent and -dependent ways (Shankar et al., 2013; Casciello et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: EHMT2 has been proposed to have oncogenic functions.
source: EHMT2 has been proposed to have oncogenic functions and its overexpression in leukemia, gastric, lung, prostate cancer, and alveolar RMS causes silencing of tumor suppressor genes through its H3K9me2 activity (Shankar et al., 2013; Casciello et al., 2015; Bhat et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Overexpression of EHMT2 in leukemia, gastric, lung, prostate cancer, and alveolar RMS causes silencing of tumor suppressor genes through its H3K9me2 activity.
source: EHMT2 has been proposed to have oncogenic functions and its overexpression in leukemia, gastric, lung, prostate cancer, and alveolar RMS causes silencing of tumor suppressor genes through its H3K9me2 activity (Shankar et al., 2013; Casciello et al., 2015; Bhat et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: EHMT2 is overexpressed in ARMS.
source: We recently reported that EHMT2 is overexpressed in ARMS (Bhat et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature from the authors' previous work

claim: EHMT2 shows high nuclear expression in 16 ERMS patient tumor sections relative to normal muscle.
source: High nuclear expression relative to normal muscle was apparent (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A

claim: EHMT2 is overexpressed at both mRNA and protein levels in three ERMS patient-derived cell lines RD18, JR1, and RD compared to primary human skeletal muscle myoblasts (HSMMs).
source: In addition, compared to primary human skeletal muscle myoblasts (HSMMs), EHMT2 overexpression at both mRNA and protein levels was apparent in three ERMS patient-derived cell lines RD18, JR1, and RD (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: Drugs targeting BRD4, PRMT5, and EHMT2 showed a strong effect on viability of JR1 and RD cell lines.
source: Drugs targeting BRD4, PRMT5, and EHMT2 showed a strong effect on viability of both cell lines (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by drug screening data shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: UNC0642 showed significantly higher efficacy against RD cells when compared to HSMM in cell viability assays.
source: Strikingly, UNC0642 showed significantly higher efficacy against RD cells when compared to HSMM in cell viability assays (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Treatment of both JR1 and RD cells with UNC0642 led to a striking reduction in colony formation.
source: Consistent with our drug screening assay, treatment of both JR1 and RD cells with UNC0642, a small molecule inhibitor of EHMT2 led to a striking reduction in colony formation (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 1G

claim: EHMT2 is overexpressed and functionally relevant in ERMS.
source: Together, these results indicate that EHMT2 is overexpressed and functionally relevant in ERMS.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including IHC, qPCR, western blot, and drug screening data

claim: EHMT2 knockdown in RD18, JR1, and RD cells resulted in increased myogenic differentiation as evidenced from increased MHC expression and MYOG expression.
source: EHMT2 knockdown (siEHMT2 cells) as well as UNC0642 treatment resulted in increased myogenic differentiation relative to their respective controls as evidenced from the increased MHC expression, a terminal differentiation marker, as well as MYOG, an early differentiation marker (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence, western blot, and qPCR data shown in Figure 2C and supplements

claim: UNC0642 treatment resulted in increased myogenic differentiation as evidenced from increased MHC expression and MYOG expression.
source: EHMT2 knockdown (siEHMT2 cells) as well as UNC0642 treatment resulted in increased myogenic differentiation relative to their respective controls as evidenced from the increased MHC expression, a terminal differentiation marker, as well as MYOG, an early differentiation marker (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence, western blot, and qPCR data shown in Figure 2C and supplements

claim: Both siEHMT2 cells and UNC0642 treatment resulted in a significant decrease in BrdU+ cells compared to their respective control in RD18 cells.
source: Both siEHMT2 cells and UNC0642 treatment resulted in a significant decrease in BrdU+ cells compared to their respective control in RD18 cells (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 2D and supplements

claim: Stable EHMT2 knockdown in RD cells resulted in increased MHC levels and decreased BrdU+ cells.
source: Further, stable EHMT2 knockdown in RD cells also resulted in increased MHC levels and decreased BrdU+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: Supported by western blot and BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 2 supplement 2E-G

claim: A striking reduction in colony formation was seen in shEHMT2 RD cells compared to controls.
source: A striking reduction in colony formation was also seen in shEHMT2 RD cells compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 2 supplement 2H

claim: EHMT2 inhibition permits cells to exit the cell cycle and undergo myogenic differentiation.
source: Together, these results indicate that EHMT2 inhibition permits cells to exit the cell cycle and undergo myogenic differentiation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing increased differentiation and decreased proliferation upon EHMT2 inhibition

claim: 872 genes were significantly upregulated in siEHMT2 cells compared to the control, of which 494 genes had a fold change >1.2.
source: Volcano plot of differentially expressed genes (Figure 3B) revealed that 872 genes were significantly upregulated in siEHMT2 cells compared to the control, of which 494 genes had a fold change >1.2.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Among the 1098 genes that were significantly downregulated in siEHMT2 cells, 695 genes had a fold change >1.2.
source: Among the 1098 genes that were significantly downregulated in siEHMT2 cells, 695 genes had a fold change >1.2.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data analysis

claim: Among the top 20 unique biological processes associated with differentially expressed genes in siEHMT2 cells were cell cycle progression and Wnt signaling.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis showed that among the top 20 unique biological processes associated with differentially expressed genes in siEHMT2 cells were cell cycle progression and Wnt signaling (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Negative regulators of the Wnt pathway such as DKK1, DKK3, and ITGA3 were downregulated in siEHMT2 cells.
source: Interestingly, negative regulators of the Wnt pathway such as DKK1, DKK3, and ITGA3 (Shukrun et al., 2014; Kato et al., 2011) were downregulated in siEHMT2 cells, whereas positive regulators such as WNT3 and FRAT2 were upregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3 supplement 1A and B

claim: Positive regulators of the Wnt pathway such as WNT3 and FRAT2 were upregulated in siEHMT2 cells.
source: Interestingly, negative regulators of the Wnt pathway such as DKK1, DKK3, and ITGA3 (Shukrun et al., 2014; Kato et al., 2011) were downregulated in siEHMT2 cells, whereas positive regulators such as WNT3 and FRAT2 were upregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3 supplement 1A and B

claim: Downregulation of DKK1 mRNA was apparent in RD18 siEHMT2 cells compared to control cells by qPCR.
source: Consistent with the transcriptomic data, downregulation of DKK1 mRNA was apparent in RD18 siEHMT2 cells compared to control cells by qPCR (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D

claim: UNC0642 treatment resulted in a decrease in DKK1 mRNA expression in RD18 cells.
source: Interestingly UNC0642 treatment also resulted in a decrease in DKK1 mRNA expression in RD18 cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E

claim: DKK1 protein levels decreased in both siEHMT2 and UNC0642 RD18-treated cells.
source: DKK1 protein levels also decreased in both siEHMT2 and UNC0642 RD18-treated cells (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F and G

claim: The reduction in DKK1 levels correlated with increased active-ß-catenin in siEHMT2 cells in RD18, RD shEHMT2 cells and upon UNC0642 treatment in RD18.
source: Moreover, the reduction in DKK1 levels correlated with increased active-ß-catenin in siEHMT2 cells (Figure 3H) in RD18, RD shEHMT2 cells (Figure 3I) and upon UNC0642 treatment in RD18 (Figure 3J) when compared to their respective controls.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3H, I, and J

claim: Loss of EHMT2 leads to downregulation of DKK1 with concomitant activation of canonical Wnt signaling and myogenic differentiation.
source: These results indicate that loss of EHMT2 leads to downregulation of DKK1 with concomitant activation of canonical Wnt signaling and myogenic differentiation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing DKK1 downregulation, active β-catenin increase, and differentiation upon EHMT2 loss

claim: EHMT2 enrichment was found mostly at gene promoters.
source: EHMT2 enrichment was found mostly at gene promoters (Figure 4A) and its occupancy was apparent at the DKK1 promoter (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A

claim: EHMT2 occupancy was apparent at the DKK1 promoter.
source: EHMT2 enrichment was found mostly at gene promoters (Figure 4A) and its occupancy was apparent at the DKK1 promoter (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B

claim: A significant enrichment of EHMT2 was seen at the DKK1 promoter by ChIP-PCR in RD18 cells.
source: To validate these results, ChIP-PCR was done in RD18 cells. A significant enrichment was seen indicating that EHMT2 directly binds to the DKK1 promoter (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4C

claim: EHMT2 directly binds to the DKK1 promoter.
source: To validate these results, ChIP-PCR was done in RD18 cells. A significant enrichment was seen indicating that EHMT2 directly binds to the DKK1 promoter (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Chromatin regions before and after the EHMT2 peak at the DKK1 promoter showed no significant EHMT2 enrichment.
source: To further ascertain the specificity of EHMT2 occupancy at the DKK1 promoter, we performed ChIP-PCR at chromatin regions before and after the EHMT2 peak at the promoter. Neither region showed significant EHMT2 enrichment (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4D and E

claim: KLF7 was one of the top DNA motifs associated with EHMT2-predicted binding sites.
source: Homer analysis of the ChIP-seq data for DNA motif enrichment at predicted EHMT2 binding sites revealed KLF7 as one of the top DNA motifs associated with EHMT2-predicted binding sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Homer analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4 supplement 1A

claim: Sp1 occupancy was detected at the DKK1 promoter in RD18 cells.
source: Consistent with these studies, Sp1 occupancy was detected at the DKK1 promoter (Figure 4F) in RD18 cells.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Both Sp1 and p300 enrichment were decreased upon treatment with UNC0642 compared to control RD18 cells.
source: Intriguingly, both Sp1 and p300 enrichment were decreased upon treatment with UNC0642 compared to control RD18 cells.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data

claim: A reduction in H3K9ac, a mark of transcriptional activation, was apparent in RD18 cells upon UNC0642 treatment.
source: Correspondingly, a reduction in H3K9ac, a mark of transcriptional activation, was apparent in RD18 cells (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4G-I

claim: A decrease in p300 and H3K9ac occupancy was observed in shEHMT2 RD cells.
source: A decrease in p300 and H3K9ac occupancy was also observed in shEHMT2 RD cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 4 supplement 1B and C

claim: The interaction between Sp1 and p300 decreased upon UNC0642 treatment in both RD18 and RD cell lines, as well as in HSMM.
source: The interaction between Sp1 and p300 decreased upon UNC0642 treatment in both RD18 and RD cell lines, as well as in HSMM (Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 4J and Figure 4 supplement 1D and E

claim: EHMT2-Sp1 and EHMT2-p300 interaction remained unchanged upon UNC0642 treatment.
source: However, EHMT2-Sp1 and EHMT2-p300 interaction remained unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 4 supplement 1F and G

claim: Immunoprecipitation with anti-Sp1 antibody confirmed a decrease in p300 association upon UNC0642 treatment.
source: To validate the PLA data, we examined Sp1–p300 interaction under UNC0642 treatment in RD cells by immunoprecipitation assays. Immunoprecipitation with anti-Sp1 antibody confirmed a decrease in p300 association upon UNC0642 treatment (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4K

claim: EHMT2 binding at the promoter results in increased Sp1 and p300 occupancy and active transcription of DKK1.
source: Thus, our results indicate that EHMT2 binding at the promoter results in increased Sp1 and p300 occupancy and active transcription of DKK1.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from ChIP-PCR, PLA, and IP data showing EHMT2 occupancy at DKK1 promoter and its impact on Sp1/p300 recruitment

claim: DKK1 was overexpressed in all three ERMS cell lines compared to HSMM at both mRNA and protein levels.
source: Correlating with high endogenous EHMT2 expression, DKK1 was also overexpressed in all three lines compared to HSMM at both mRNA and protein levels (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: DKK1 knockdown in RD18 cells resulted in an increase in active-ß-catenin levels.
source: Similar to EHMT2 knockdown, DKK1 knockdown in RD18 cells resulted in an increase in active-ß-catenin levels indicating an upregulation of canonical Wnt signaling (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C

claim: DKK1 knockdown in RD18 cells resulted in a significant decrease in BrdU+ cells compared to control cells.
source: Moreover, analogous to EHMT2 knockdown, DKK1 knockdown in RD18 cells resulted in a significant decrease in BrdU+ cells compared to control cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 5D

claim: DKK1 knockdown resulted in increased differentiation as evidenced by elevated MHC levels and MYOG expression in RD18 cells.
source: A corresponding increase in differentiation was also apparent by elevated MHC levels and MYOG expression in RD18 cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by western blot, immunofluorescence, and qPCR data shown in Figure 5E

claim: A similar decrease in BrdU+ cells and increase in MHC levels upon DKK1 knockdown were observed in RD cells.
source: A similar decrease in BrdU+ cells and increase in MHC levels upon DKK1 knockdown were observed in RD cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation assay and western blot data shown in Figure 5 supplement 1A and B

claim: Recombinant DKK1 (rDKK1) added to siEHMT2 cells resulted in the reduction of active β-catenin seen in siEHMT2 cells.
source: Recombinant DKK1 (rDKK1) was added to siEHMT2 cells for 24 hr that resulted in the reduction of active β-catenin seen in siEHMT2 cells.
evidence: Supported by western blot data from rescue experiment

claim: In the presence of rDKK1, the increase in MHC+ cells and MYOG expression in siEHMT2 cells was reversed to control levels.
source: Interestingly, in the presence of rDKK1, the increase in MHC+ cells and MYOG expression in siEHMT2 cells was reversed to control levels.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and qPCR data from rescue experiment

claim: The decrease in BrdU+ cells upon EHMT2 knockdown were restored to levels comparable to control in the presence of rDKK1.
source: Similarly, the decrease in BrdU+ cells upon EHMT2 knockdown were restored to levels comparable to control (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 5F

claim: LGK974 reversed the effects of EHMT2 knockdown on proliferation, differentiation, and active β-catenin levels.
source: Similar to rDKK1, LGK974 reversed the effects of EHMT2 knockdown on proliferation, differentiation, and active β-catenin levels (Figure 5G) indicating that EHMT2 mediates the differentiation block by activating DKK1 expression that in turn suppresses canonical Wnt signaling.
evidence: Supported by western blot, immunofluorescence, qPCR, and BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 5G

claim: EHMT2 mediates the differentiation block by activating DKK1 expression that in turn suppresses canonical Wnt signaling.
source: Similar to rDKK1, LGK974 reversed the effects of EHMT2 knockdown on proliferation, differentiation, and active β-catenin levels (Figure 5G) indicating that EHMT2 mediates the differentiation block by activating DKK1 expression that in turn suppresses canonical Wnt signaling.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from rescue experiments with rDKK1 and LGK974

claim: Treatment with UNC0642 resulted in reduced tumor growth compared to the control group in RD cell xenografts without any significant changes in body weight.
source: Treatment with UNC0642 resulted in reduced tumor growth compared to the control group without any significant changes in body weight (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figure 6A

claim: H3K9me2 decreased in tumors from mice treated with UNC0642.
source: By immunohistochemical analysis (Figure 6B) we confirmed a decrease in H3K9me2 in tumors from mice treated with UNC0642 indicating efficacy of the drug in vivo.
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The proliferation marker Ki67 was decreased in tumors from mice treated with UNC0642.
source: The proliferation marker Ki67 was decreased, whereas MHC+ cells were increased in tumors from mice treated with UNC0642.
evidence: Supported by IHC data

claim: MHC+ cells were increased in tumors from mice treated with UNC0642.
source: The proliferation marker Ki67 was decreased, whereas MHC+ cells were increased in tumors from mice treated with UNC0642.
evidence: Supported by IHC data

claim: DKK1 was decreased upon UNC0642 treatment in tumors, and correspondingly active-ß-catenin levels were elevated.
source: Moreover, DKK1 was decreased upon UNC0642 treatment, and correspondingly active-ß-catenin levels were elevated (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Tumor volume in mice injected with shEHMT2 cells was reduced compared to the control group.
source: Tumor volume in mice injected with shEHMT2 cells was reduced compared to the control group.
evidence: Supported by in vivo xenograft data

claim: Mice injected with shEHMT2 cells and treated with LGK974 showed tumor volumes comparable to the control group.
source: However, mice injected with shEHMT2 cells and treated with LGK974 showed tumor volumes comparable to the control group.
evidence: Supported by in vivo xenograft data

claim: Body weight of mice did not show any significant changes over the course of treatment with LGK974.
source: Body weight of mice did not show any significant changes over the course of this treatment.
evidence: Supported by in vivo xenograft data

claim: EHMT2 expression was decreased in mice injected with shEHMT2 cells that correlated with decrease in Ki67+ cells and increase in MHC+ cells compared to tumors of the control group.
source: As expected, EHMT2 expression was decreased in mice injected with shEHMT2 cells that correlated with decrease in Ki67+ cells and increase in MHC+ cells compared to tumors of the control group.
evidence: Supported by IHC data

claim: The alteration in Ki67 and MHC upon EHMT2 knockdown was not seen in the tumors from mice injected with shEHMT2 cells that underwent LGK974 treatment.
source: This alteration was however not seen in the tumors from mice injected with shEHMT2 cells that underwent LGK974 treatment.
evidence: Supported by IHC data

claim: The reduction in DKK1 and increase in active-ß-catenin in tumors from shEHMT2 injected mice were reversed upon LGK974 treatment.
source: Consistently, the reduction in DKK1 and increase in active-ß-catenin in tumors from shEHMT2 injected mice were reversed in upon LGK974 treatment (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Inhibition of EHMT2 expression or activity promotes differentiation and reduces tumor progression by regulating Wnt signaling.
source: Taken together, our studies demonstrate that inhibition of EHMT2 expression or activity promotes differentiation and reduces tumor progression by regulating Wnt signaling.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple in vitro and in vivo experimental results

claim: Integration of RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data showed many genes involved in myogenic differentiation, cell cycle progression, and metabolic pathways to be directly or indirectly regulated by EHMT2.
source: Integration of RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) showed many genes involved in myogenic differentiation, cell cycle progression, and metabolic pathways (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F) to be directly or indirectly regulated by EHMT2.
evidence: Supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5 supplement 1C-F

claim: Genes involved in myogenic differentiation, cell cycle progression, and metabolic pathways, independent of Wnt signaling, may contribute to oncogenic effects of EHMT2 in ERMS cells.
source: These genes, independent of Wnt signaling, may contribute to oncogenic effects of EHMT2 in ERMS cells.
evidence: Speculation based on RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data analysis

claim: EHMT2 suppresses canonical Wnt signaling by activating expression of the Wnt antagonist DKK1.
source: We demonstrate that EHMT2 suppresses canonical Wnt signaling by activating expression of the Wnt antagonist DKK1.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing EHMT2 regulation of DKK1 and Wnt signaling

claim: Inhibition of EHMT2 expression or activity in human ERMS cell lines reduced DKK1 expression and elevated canonical Wnt signaling resulting in myogenic differentiation in vitro.
source: Inhibition of EHMT2 expression or activity in human ERMS cell lines reduced DKK1 expression and elevated canonical Wnt signaling resulting in myogenic differentiation in vitro and in mouse xenograft models in vivo.
evidence: Supported by multiple in vitro experimental results including knockdown, inhibitor treatment, and differentiation assays

claim: Inhibition of EHMT2 expression or activity in human ERMS cell lines reduced DKK1 expression and elevated canonical Wnt signaling resulting in myogenic differentiation in mouse xenograft models in vivo.
source: Inhibition of EHMT2 expression or activity in human ERMS cell lines reduced DKK1 expression and elevated canonical Wnt signaling resulting in myogenic differentiation in vitro and in mouse xenograft models in vivo.
evidence: Supported by in vivo xenograft experimental results

claim: EHMT2 impacted Sp1 and p300 enrichment at the DKK1 promoter.
